# What this workshop is about

Bulk RNA-seq measures the average of all cells in a sample. Single-cell
RNA-seq measures each cell separately, so we can ask which cell types are
present, in which proportions, and in which states. The measurements are
sparse and noisy: a zero can mean the gene was off, or that its molecules were
not captured.

Library preparation, alignment, and counting are done. You start from a Seurat
object with a count matrix and sample information and turn it into cell types
you can defend.

By the end, you should be able to:

- tell apart genes, cells, samples, and people;
- explain what QC, normalisation, PCA, clustering, and UMAP each contribute;
- name clusters from marker evidence, and leave a cluster unnamed when the
  evidence is mixed;
- check which samples a cluster comes from before calling it a cell type.

The sequence follows **Mert Cihan's “Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Data Analysis
with Seurat”**, just in a very swmall and quick workshop

## Your route

Open **student_workbook.R**. Exercise 1 loads the data with supplied code.
From Exercise 2 on, each step has a task and an **AI prompt**: let a free
chatbot write the code, read it, run it in your workbook, and answer the
questions below it. The prompts name the settings to use, so that your
clusters match the checkpoints and the solutions. If the code does not work or
time runs short, open **Show the code** below the prompt and use the supplied
version. If a step fails completely, load the checkpoint named in that step.

An AI assistant can write and explain code, or discuss a plot you describe to
it. Do not ask it to invent sample information or to name clusters it cannot see.
It might also accidentaly fool you to believe something that isnt there, so watch out.

## The data

Real human subventricular-zone tissue from **GSE248995**: 15 people undergoing
brain-tumour surgery, one sample each. Not every cell in a sample is a tumour
cell. See [Baig et al., 2024](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10940989/)
and the [GEO record](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE248995).

The full object has 18,734 genes and 10,834 cells. To keep computation short we
took at most 100 random cells per sample, before looking at any clusters:
**1,344 cells from 15 samples**, original counts, all genes. Rare cell types can
be missed, and the cap changes the overall proportions, so do not use this
subset to estimate the complete tissue composition.

| Metadata | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `sample_id` | GEO accession of the sample |
| `sample_label` | Sample name from the original workshop |
| `nCount_RNA` | Total counts (UMIs) per cell |
| `nFeature_RNA` | Number of genes detected per cell |
| `percent.mt` | Percentage of counts from mitochondrial genes |

There are no treatment groups, outcomes, or time points. The question is:
**which cell populations are present, and what evidence supports each name?**

# Exercise 1 / Inspect the object

```{r load-object}
source("start_here.R")
sc
dim(sc)
head(sc[[]])
table(sc$sample_label)
```

The count matrix has genes in rows and cells in columns. `sc[[]]` returns the
cell metadata: one row per cell, in the same order as the matrix columns.

<div class="checkpoint">
<strong>Before proceeding:</strong> how many genes, cells, and samples are
there? Why do two samples have fewer than 100 cells? Why are 1,344 cells not
1,344 independent observations for a statement about people?
</div>

# Exercise 2 / Quality control

Not every barcode holds one intact cell:

- a **damaged cell** has lost cytoplasmic RNA: few genes, and a high share of
  mitochondrial counts;
- an **empty droplet** holds only free-floating RNA: very few genes;
- a **doublet** captured two cells: unusually *many* genes and counts.

Free-floating (**ambient**) RNA from burst cells also lands in intact cells. No
filter removes it; you will meet it again in Exercise 5.

Two filtering rules are on the table:

| Rule | Detected genes | Mitochondrial share |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Working rule | more than 200 and fewer than 6,000 | below 20% |
| Strict standard rule (from the longer workshop) | more than 200 and fewer than 2,500 | below 5% |

**Your task:** look at the QC distributions per sample, compare what the two
rules would keep, then apply the working rule.

Try your own prompt, or look at the Seurat tutrial from their webpage if you want a more hardcore experience. this is how it could look though:

> **AI prompt:** My Seurat object is called sc (Seurat 5). Its metadata has
> sample_label, nFeature_RNA, nCount_RNA, and percent.mt. Write R code that
> (1) draws violin plots of the three QC columns by sample_label, without points;
> (2) plots nCount_RNA against nFeature_RNA, coloured by sample_label;
> (3) prints a summary of the three columns; (4) counts per sample_label how
> many cells each of the two rules in the table keeps. Then keep only the cells
> that pass the working rule, still in sc.

<details>
<summary>Show the code</summary>

```{r qc-plots}
VlnPlot(sc, features = c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt"),
        group.by = "sample_label", pt.size = 0, ncol = 3, layer = "counts")
FeatureScatter(sc, feature1 = "nCount_RNA", feature2 = "nFeature_RNA",
               group.by = "sample_label")
summary(sc[[]][, c("nFeature_RNA", "nCount_RNA", "percent.mt")])
```

```{r qc-rules}
qc <- sc[[]]
qc$keep_working <- with(qc, nFeature_RNA > 200 & nFeature_RNA < 6000 & percent.mt < 20)
qc$keep_strict  <- with(qc, nFeature_RNA > 200 & nFeature_RNA < 2500 & percent.mt < 5)
colSums(qc[, c("keep_working", "keep_strict")])
aggregate(cbind(keep_working, keep_strict) ~ sample_label, qc, sum)
```

```{r qc-apply}
sc <- subset(sc, cells = rownames(qc)[qc$keep_working])
ncol(sc)
```

</details>

Look at the smallest values in `summary()`: these data were already filtered
before they reached us.

> **task:** Describe your scatter plot (where most cells
> sit, where the outliers are) and ask what a doublet and a damaged cell would
> look like in it.

<div class="checkpoint">
<strong>Before proceeding:</strong> how many cells does each rule keep, and
which samples would lose most under the strict rule? Is a rule that removes
more cells better? Which barcode problem can neither rule catch?
</div>

**Stuck?** `sc <- readRDS("checkpoints/brain_cells_qc.rds")` loads the filtered cells.

# Exercise 3 / Normalise and run PCA

> **AI prompt:** sc holds raw counts after QC (Quality Control. Write Seurat code that
> log-normalises the counts, finds 2,000 variable genes, scales them, and runs a
> PCA with 30 components and seed.use = 42. Keep the object name sc. Then plot
> the PCA coloured by sample_label and an elbow plot of the 30 components.

<details>
<summary>Show the code</summary>

```{r pca}
sc <- NormalizeData(sc, verbose = FALSE)
sc <- FindVariableFeatures(sc, nfeatures = 2000, verbose = FALSE)
sc <- ScaleData(sc, verbose = FALSE)
sc <- RunPCA(sc, npcs = 30, seed.use = 42, verbose = FALSE)
DimPlot(sc, reduction = "pca", group.by = "sample_label")
ElbowPlot(sc, ndims = 30)
```

</details>

- **NormalizeData** divides each cell's counts by its total and log-transforms
  them, so cells with more counts become comparable to cells with fewer.
- **FindVariableFeatures** keeps the 2,000 genes that vary most between cells.
- **ScaleData** centres and scales these genes so that no single gene
  dominates the PCA.
- **RunPCA** summarises them into 30 components, as in the training.

The elbow plot shows the standard deviation of each PC; where the curve
flattens, further PCs add little. We use **PCs 1–15**. That is a working
choice, not the optimum for every Seurat run and can change between every dataset.

<div class="checkpoint">
<strong>Before proceeding:</strong> are variable genes the same as
differentially expressed genes? Does normalisation remove sample effects?
What could you lose with 5 PCs, and what could you add with 30?
</div>

# Exercise 4 / Clusters and UMAP

Seurat connects each cell to its most similar neighbours in PCA space, then
finds groups of densely connected cells. The **resolution** sets how finely it
splits. UMAP draws the same neighbourhoods in two dimensions.

Again, try yourself at a prompt. But this one should generally work. Make sure
you know what resolution, PCA dims and so on mean.

> **AI prompt:** sc has a PCA. Using PCs 1 to 15, build the neighbour graph,
> find clusters at resolution 0.4 with random.seed = 42, and run UMAP with
> seed.use = 42. Then copy sc to sc_more, recluster the copy at resolution 1.0,
> and plot both clusterings side by side on the same UMAP, with cluster
> numbers. Finally colour the UMAP of sc by sample_label.

<details>
<summary>Show the code</summary>

```{r clustering}
sc <- FindNeighbors(sc, dims = 1:15, verbose = FALSE)
sc <- FindClusters(sc, resolution = 0.4, random.seed = 42, verbose = FALSE)
sc <- RunUMAP(sc, dims = 1:15, seed.use = 42, verbose = FALSE)
sc_more <- FindClusters(sc, resolution = 1.0, random.seed = 42, verbose = FALSE)
(DimPlot(sc, label = TRUE) + ggtitle("Resolution 0.4")) +
  (DimPlot(sc_more, label = TRUE) + ggtitle("Resolution 1.0"))
DimPlot(sc, group.by = "sample_label")
```

</details>

Both clusterings are drawn on the same UMAP, so only the grouping differs.
Clusters and UMAP come from the same PCs. 

<div class="checkpoint">
<strong>Before proceeding:</strong> how many clusters does each resolution
give? Does a finer split mean better biology? In the sample-coloured UMAP,
which groups look like they come from a single sample?
</div>

**Stuck?** `sc <- readRDS("checkpoints/brain_cells_umap.rds")` loads the cells
clustered at resolution 0.4. We continue with resolution 0.4.

# Exercise 5 / Name the cell types

Clusters are numbered, not named. A cluster gets a name when it expresses
**several** markers of one cell type and few of the others. Start with the
short marker panel in `data/marker_reference.csv`:

> **AI prompt:** data/marker_reference.csv has the columns gene_id and
> population. Read it, print which genes belong to which population, and make
> a Seurat DotPlot of all its genes, in the order of the file, for the clusters
> in sc, with rotated axis labels.

<details>
<summary>Show the code</summary>

```{r dotplot}
panel <- read.csv("data/marker_reference.csv")
split(panel$gene_id, panel$population)  # which genes mark which population
DotPlot(sc, features = panel$gene_id) + RotatedAxis()
```

</details>

The genes are ordered by population, in the order of the file. Dot size is the
share of cells in the cluster that express the gene; colour is the average
expression, scaled per gene, so each gene's colours show where it is highest.
Then check what the data themselves say: `FindAllMarkers()` compares each
cluster with all other cells.

Try yourself with a prompt or use this one (what do the variables mean?)

> **AI prompt:** Run FindAllMarkers on sc for positive markers only
> (min.pct = 0.25, logfc.threshold = 0.25). Then make a table with one row per
> cluster: the number of cells and the five genes with the highest avg_log2FC
> among genes with p_val_adj < 0.05, leaving out gene names that contain a dot
> (unnamed clones such as RP11-552D4.1). Save it as output/top5_markers.csv.

<details>
<summary>Show the code</summary>

```{r discover-markers}
cluster_markers <- FindAllMarkers(sc, only.pos = TRUE, min.pct = 0.25,
                                  logfc.threshold = 0.25, verbose = FALSE)
# If this takes too long: cluster_markers <- read.csv("output/cluster_markers.csv")
named <- subset(cluster_markers, p_val_adj < 0.05 & !grepl(".", gene, fixed = TRUE))
top5 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(named, named$cluster), function(d) {
  d <- head(d[order(-d$avg_log2FC), ], 5)
  data.frame(cluster = d$cluster[1], cells = sum(Idents(sc) == d$cluster[1]),
             top_genes = paste(d$gene, collapse = ", "))
}))
top5
write.csv(top5, "output/top5_markers.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

</details>

The table lists, for each cluster, the five genes that most distinguish it from
all other cells. A top gene can mark a cell type, a cell state, or something
specific to one person. These tests reuse the data that made the clusters, so
their p-values do not validate the clusters. This is also a simplified version of 
how this normally works

Use both sources: the panel shows known markers; the top-5 list shows what the
data themselves emphasise. Look up unfamiliar genes (GeneCards, the Human
Protein Atlas, or a search engine), or ask an assistant:

> **AI task:** Copy your top-5 table as text (not as a file) into a chatbot
> and ask which cell type or cell state each gene list suggests in human brain
> tissue removed during surgery. Treat the answers as suggestions: check each
> one in the dot plot or with `FeaturePlot(sc, features = c("GENE1", "GENE2"))`
> before you use it.

Now name every cluster. Two clusters can share a name. Write **"Unassigned"** or mark them as a mix of cell types.
When the markers are mixed that is a valid result.

```{r name-clusters}
cluster_names <- c("0" = "...", "1" = "...", "2" = "...", "3" = "...", "4" = "...",
                   "5" = "...", "6" = "...", "7" = "...", "8" = "...")
sc$cell_type <- unname(cluster_names[as.character(Idents(sc))])
table(sc$cell_type, useNA = "ifany")
DimPlot(sc, group.by = "cell_type", label = TRUE, repel = TRUE)
write.csv(data.frame(cluster = names(cluster_names), cell_type = cluster_names),
          "output/my_cell_types.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

<div class="checkpoint">
<strong>Before proceeding:</strong> which clusters could you name with at
least two markers? Which did you leave unassigned, and why? The red-blood-cell
genes HBA1 and HBB are detected in many clusters. Are all these cells red
blood cells?
</div>

# Exercise 6 / Where do the clusters come from?

A cell type should appear in several people. A cluster made by one sample can
be a cell type only that person has, a state of that person's cells, or a
technical artefact of that sample.

> **AI prompt:** sc has clusters (Idents(sc)) and the metadata columns
> sample_label and cell_type. Make a table of cluster by sample_label, and print
> for each cluster the share of its cells that come from its largest sample.
> Then draw a ggplot2 bar chart with one bar per sample_label, filled by
> cell_type, showing proportions, with readable x-axis labels.

<details>
<summary>Show the code</summary>

```{r composition}
composition <- table(cluster = Idents(sc), sample = sc$sample_label)
composition
round(apply(composition, 1, max) / rowSums(composition), 2)  # share from the largest sample
ggplot(sc[[]], aes(x = sample_label, fill = cell_type)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of cells", fill = "Cell type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 60, hjust = 1))
```

</details>

<div class="checkpoint">
<strong>Before proceeding:</strong> which clusters come almost entirely from
one sample? For each of them, look back at its markers: is it a cell type, a
state, or an artefact, and what would you need to decide? Is a
sample-specific cluster automatically a batch effect that integration should
remove?
</div>

Integration methods (CCA, Harmony) align shared cell types across samples. They
can also erase a population or a state that really exists in only one person.
Inspect sample composition first, as you did here, and integrate only with a
reason.

# Exercise 7 / Conclude

Save your workbook, your cell-type table, and one figure, for example:

```{r save-figure}
ggsave("output/my_cell_types.png",
       DimPlot(sc, group.by = "cell_type", label = TRUE, repel = TRUE),
       width = 8, height = 5)
```

<div class="checkpoint">
<strong>Send Ava:</strong> four short statements.
(1) Your QC decision and what it changed.
(2) What changed when the resolution increased.
(3) One cell-type name and the markers that support it.
(4) One cluster you could not name, and the evidence you would need.
</div>

::: {.key-ideas}
**Key ideas · Single cells**

- One sample is one person. Many cells from one person describe that person in
  detail; they do not replace more people.
- QC removes barcodes that are not intact single cells; doublets and ambient
  RNA partly survive it.
- Normalisation → variable genes → scaling → PCA → neighbours → clusters →
  UMAP. Each step contains choices (PCs, resolution) that change the clusters.
- A cell-type name needs several markers. Unassigned is an honest answer.
- Check which samples a cluster comes from before naming it, and before
  integrating samples.
:::
